# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke, conferring a four- to fivefold increased risk [1]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC) with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) remains the cornerstone of thromboembolic prophylaxis [2]. However, a substantial proportion of patients have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation or experience major bleeding, creating a therapeutic dilemma [3]. Because approximately 90% of thrombi in nonvalvular AF originate in the left atrial appendage (LAA), mechanical exclusion of this structure offers an attractive nonpharmacological alternative [4]. Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has therefore emerged as an established intervention for stroke prevention in selected patients [5].

## Rationale and Anatomy

The LAA is a trabeculated, embryologically distinct remnant of the primitive left atrium with highly variable morphology, classified as "chicken wing," "windsock," "cactus," or "cauliflower" types [6]. This morphological diversity influences both thrombogenicity and procedural planning [7]. Reduced appendage emptying velocities during AF promote stasis and thrombus formation, providing the pathophysiological basis for closure [4]. Preprocedural imaging with transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and cardiac computed tomography is essential for sizing and exclusion of pre-existing thrombus [8].

## Devices and Technique

Two dominant endocardial device families have shaped contemporary practice. The Watchman device (and its successor Watchman FLX) is a parachute-shaped nitinol frame deployed via transseptal access [9]. The Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and its iteration, the Amulet, employ a distinct lobe-and-disc design enabling closure of varied anatomies [10]. Epicardial approaches, such as the LARIAT suture ligation system, achieve closure without leaving an endocardial implant but carry distinct procedural risks [11]. Procedural success rates exceeding 95% are now routinely reported in high-volume centers [12].

## Pivotal Clinical Trials

The evidence base for endocardial LAAC rests primarily on two randomized trials comparing the Watchman device with warfarin. PROTECT AF demonstrated noninferiority of LAAC to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, albeit with early procedural complications [13]. The subsequent PREVAIL trial addressed safety concerns and confirmed improved procedural outcomes [14]. Five-year pooled analyses of both trials showed comparable stroke prevention with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality compared with warfarin [15,16]. The PRAGUE-17 trial extended this evidence by comparing LAAC with DOACs in high-risk patients, demonstrating noninferiority [17]. More recently, the Amulet IDE trial established noninferiority of the Amulet device to the Watchman for safety and efficacy endpoints [18].

## Periprocedural Management and Complications

Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in approximately 3–4% of patients and is associated with increased thromboembolic risk [19]. Peri-device leak, often identified on follow-up imaging, has uncertain long-term significance, though larger leaks may warrant continued anticoagulation [20]. Major complications include pericardial effusion and tamponade, device embolization, and vascular injury, the incidence of which has declined with operator experience and device refinement [21]. Optimal antithrombotic regimens following implantation remain debated, ranging from short-term DOAC therapy to dual antiplatelet therapy, with ongoing studies evaluating single antiplatelet strategies [22,23].

## Guidelines and Patient Selection

Current European and American guidelines assign LAAC a role in patients with nonvalvular AF and contraindications to long-term anticoagulation [24,25]. Real-world registries, including the EWOLUTION registry and the US National Cardiovascular Data Registry LAAO Registry, have confirmed favorable safety and efficacy in broad populations treated outside trial conditions [26,27]. Patient selection should incorporate stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) and bleeding risk (HAS-BLED) assessment, alongside anatomical suitability [28].

## Future Directions

Several questions remain unresolved. Randomized trials comparing LAAC directly with DOACs in patients eligible for anticoagulation, such as CHAMPION-AF and CATALYST, are ongoing and will clarify the role of closure as a first-line alternative [29]. Concurrent surgical and percutaneous LAA management, advances in imaging-guided deployment, and strategies to minimize DRT and peri-device leak represent active areas of investigation [30]. As device technology matures and operator experience accumulates, LAAC is likely to occupy an expanding niche in personalized stroke prevention.

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC has evolved from an experimental concept into an evidence-supported therapy for stroke prevention in AF, particularly for patients unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation. While randomized data establish noninferiority to warfarin and emerging comparisons with DOACs are encouraging, careful patient selection, meticulous procedural technique, and structured follow-up remain essential to optimize outcomes.
